BEYOND THE REHEARSAL; Series One When The Song Becomes a Lifeline Rediscovering the Purpose, Spiritual Responsibility and Human Impact of Gospel Music “No rehearsal should be attended casually. We are not merely preparing songs for a service; we are preparing ourselves for the responsibility of serving through music.” — Victor Adenola Introduction I was rehearsing with my church choir one evening when a man walked into the church. He had made up his mind to end his life and was on his way to carry out that decision. Somewhere along his journey, however, he heard the sound of music. Something about the sound caught his attention, and he decided to find out where it was coming from. He passed several churches before eventually arriving at the church where we were rehearsing. He entered, sat at the back, and began to weep. One of our ministers noticed him and went over to attend to him. We had been doing what choirs do. We were rehearsing songs, working through musical passages, and preparing for an upcoming ministration. We had no idea that someone outside the church was listening or that the sound of our rehearsal would become part of his journey that evening. That experience changed the way I thought about choir rehearsal. It reminded me that we may know the songs we are preparing, but we may never know the circumstances of the people who will hear them. We may never know who is struggling silently, who is searching for hope, who needs encouragement, or who simply needs to find a place where someone will listen. The music did not replace the care the man needed. Rather, it drew his attention to a place where a minister could respond to him. That distinction is important. Gospel music is not a substitute for pastoral care, professional support, or human compassion. But it can become a point of connection through which someone encounters a community prepared to care. Since that experience, I have become increasingly convinced that choir rehearsal must be approached with a deeper sense of purpose. We must move beyond the assumption that rehearsal is simply the process of learning songs for Sunday service. We must begin to understand it as preparation for a responsibility that extends beyond the choir room. Gospel Music Is More Than a Genre What makes gospel music different from other forms of music? The answer cannot be reduced to a particular rhythm, vocal style, instrument, chord progression, or the presence of Christian lyrics. Gospel music, within the context of Christian worship, carries a message. It can communicate biblical truth, express faith, proclaim gratitude, offer prayer, recount testimony, encourage perseverance, and direct the attention of the listener towards God. This gives the gospel choir a responsibility that extends beyond musical execution. A choir may sing every note correctly and still fail to communicate the message effectively. A soloist may possess an excellent voice but lack an understanding of the words being sung. An arrangement may be technically impressive yet distract from the purpose of the song. This is why musical excellence and spiritual understanding must work together. Before singing a song, we should ask ourselves: What are we saying? What do these lyrics mean? Why is this song appropriate for this moment? How can our musical interpretation communicate its message clearly? These questions should influence how we approach tempo, phrasing, dynamics, articulation, diction, tone, and ensemble balance. A song of prayer may require restraint and sensitivity. A song of celebration may call for energy and clarity. A testimony may require careful attention to the words so that the story remains understandable. The objective is not to manufacture emotion. It is to communicate the song faithfully. “The first responsibility of a gospel singer is not merely to sing the notes correctly, but to understand the message those notes are carrying.”— Victor Adenola When the choir understands the message, its musical decisions become more intentional. Members begin to see their individual contributions as part of a larger purpose. The Difference Between Performing and Ministering Performance and ministry are not enemies. A choir can perform exceptionally well and use that excellence to serve the church. The problem begins when performance becomes the entire objective. When the applause becomes more important than the message, when personal recognition overshadows collective responsibility, or when a choir is more concerned about impressing the congregation than communicating the song, something important has been misplaced. A music director must therefore ask more than whether the choir sounds impressive. Did the singers communicate the lyrics clearly? Was the arrangement appropriate? Did the accompaniment support the voices? Was the choir prepared? Did the musical choices serve the purpose of the song? These are questions of both musicianship and ministry. Spiritual sincerity does not excuse poor preparation. Equally, technical competence does not automatically establish spiritual maturity. A choir needs both. We must be willing to study, practise, accept correction, develop our voices, improve our musicianship, and learn to work together. Excellence in gospel music is not about making ourselves the centre of attention. It is about developing our gifts well enough to serve the purpose entrusted to us. Excellence is not opposed to spirituality; when pursued with humility and the right purpose, it can become an expression of responsible service. – Victor Adenola The goal is not to eliminate performance but to place performance in its proper context. The Unseen Listener: Who Might Be Hearing Your Song? A choir usually rehearses with a specific event in mind. The members know the songs, the service schedule, and the expected audience. But music does not always remain within the boundaries we imagine. Someone may hear a rehearsal from outside the church. A visitor may walk in unexpectedly. Someone listening online may be dealing with grief, uncertainty, loneliness, or disappointment. A familiar lyric may remind a person of a difficult experience or encourage them to seek help. We cannot know how every listener will respond. We should never assume that everyone who hears a gospel song will experience the same emotions or reach the same conclusions. Nevertheless, we must recognise that the people listening to our music are human beings with real lives and circumstances. Some arrive at church celebrating. Others arrive carrying burdens they cannot easily explain. Some are confident in their faith, while others are searching for answers. Some have supportive relationships, while others feel isolated even in a crowded room. Our responsibility is not to diagnose their circumstances through their reactions to music. It is to serve faithfully, communicate clearly, and treat people with dignity. The experience I shared at the beginning of this article reminds me that we may never know the full impact of our rehearsal. We may never receive a testimony. We may never know whether someone was encouraged, comforted, or moved to seek support. That uncertainty should not make us careless. It should make us humble. Imagine that man walking in only to meet the choir in a hot argument or members trading words carelessly. The outcome would have been different. “You may never know who is listening, what they are carrying, or what your music means to them. Prepare faithfully, because the value of your service is not limited to the recognition you receive.”— Victor Adenola Rehearsal Is a Place of Preparation and Formation Rehearsal is often understood as the process of repeating songs until the choir can sing them accurately. This is necessary, but it is not the whole picture. Rehearsal also forms habits, attitudes, relationships, and standards. It teaches singers to listen, cooperate, accept correction, regulate their voices, manage time, and take responsibility for a shared outcome. It teaches music directors to plan, communicate, teach, evaluate, and lead. Over time, the rehearsal environment becomes a reflection of the culture the choir has chosen to tolerate. If punctuality is valued, members learn to respect time. If preparation is expected, singers learn to take personal responsibility. If correction is delivered respectfully, members are more likely to receive it constructively. But when lateness becomes normal, preparation is neglected, or members are ridiculed for making mistakes, those behaviours can gradually become part of the choir’s culture. This is why choir leaders must pay attention to both the music and the environment in which the music is developed. Rehearsal as a battle formation In the introduction Series, I mentioned that a rehearsal is a birthplace of altar. It shouldn’t be approached casually. When altars are being created, characters are formed, attitudes are reshaped, orderliness becomes stabilized, the team becomes formidable and fully armed for spiritual music. I often think of choir rehearsal as the preparation of a team for an important assignment. A team needs a shared objective. Every member must understand their role, develop the necessary skills, coordinate with others, and work towards a common outcome. The choir is no different. The soprano, alto, tenor, bass, instrumentalist, and music director may have different responsibilities, but their contributions must work together. The purpose of this formation is not to compete against other churches or treat people as enemies. It is to prepare the choir to serve faithfully and communicate the gospel effectively. Every rehearsal should move the group closer to that objective. A choir that understands its purpose will approach rehearsal differently. It will become more deliberate about preparation, more receptive to instruction, and more concerned about the quality of its collective work. – Victor Adenola Three Dimensions of Intentional Gospel Choir Rehearsal For a choir to approach rehearsal holistically, three dimensions must work together. Spiritual Preparation Members should understand the message of the song, reflect on its purpose, and approach their responsibility with humility. This includes studying lyrics, clarifying biblical references, and understanding the role the song plays within the worship service. Spiritual preparation should not become a substitute for practical work. Rather, it should give direction to that work. 2. Musical Preparation The choir must develop the skills required to communicate the music effectively. These include pitch accuracy, rhythm, diction, breath management, vocal health, harmony, blend, balance, dynamics, phrasing, and interpretation. A music director must be able to identify weaknesses and provide practical instruction. If the choir repeatedly struggles with a particular passage, the solution may involve sectional rehearsal, slower practice, individual assignments, or a clearer demonstration of the musical material. 3. Relational Preparation A choir is a community of people, not merely a collection of voices. Members must learn to listen to one another, respect leadership, receive correction, communicate honestly, and resolve disagreements responsibly. A choir with excellent voices but a destructive culture will struggle to sustain healthy collaboration. _ Victor Adenola Relational maturity does not mean that everyone must agree about everything. It means that differences can be addressed without humiliation, hostility, or disregard for the shared objective. When spiritual understanding, musical preparation, and relational maturity work together, the choir is better equipped to serve. “A strong choir is not built by voices alone. It is built through preparation, understanding, discipline, and the willingness to work together towards a common purpose.”— Victor Adenola When Music Meets Human Need The story that inspired this series also raises a practical question: what should a choir do when someone responds to a song in a way that suggests they may need help? The answer begins with compassion and an understanding of boundaries. If someone approaches a choir member after a service to share a personal struggle, the member should listen respectfully and avoid rushing to make promises or offer simplistic explanations. The person may need pastoral support, practical assistance, professional counselling, or emergency help, depending on the circumstances. Choir members should not assume that they are qualified to handle every situation. They should know when to involve a responsible minister or the pastorate or direct someone towards appropriate professional support. If someone expresses suicidal thoughts or appears to be in immediate danger, take the situation seriously and seek urgent assistance. Where it is safe to do so, remain with the person while appropriate help is arranged. Music can be an important point of connection, but it is not a replacement for the care a person may need. This is not a limitation to be ashamed of. It is an important part of responsible ministry. The choir’s role is to prepare well, serve faithfully, and contribute to a church environment where people are treated with dignity and connected with appropriate support Conclusion No rehearsal should be attended casually—not because we expect to save everyone through music, but because the responsibility of serving through music deserves our best. And more importantly, it is a birthplace of altar where worshippers are transformed. Let us become choirs that understand the songs we sing, prepare with the seriousness the work deserves, and remain attentive to the people we serve.
